pages.title: Light pollution is getting worse, and Earth is paying the price | National Geographic
pages.description: Electric lights have revolutionized our lives, but as illumination increases, the toll on wildlife and human health is becoming harder to ignore.
pages.text: Light pollution is getting worse, and Earth is paying the price | National Geographic By Nadia Drake Photographs by Babak Tafreshi Published April 3, 2019 • 25 min read On a clear night in 1994, an earthquake rumbled beneath Los Angeles and caused a city-wide power outage just before dawn. Startled awake, some residents who had stumbled outside called various emergency centers and a local observatory to report a mysterious cloud overhead. That weird object turned out to be the band of the Milky Way , our home galaxy, which had long been obscured from view by the city’s lights. Arguably, the light bulb is the most transformative invention humans have introduced to this planet. By flicking a switch or pushing a button, we can push back the veil that would naturally shroud our lives each night. Now, we work long after the sun sinks below the horizon. We play games outside until the hours stretch into double digits. We more safely roam city streets after dark. ( Opinion: Bright Nights, Big Problems) The city of Las Vegas dumps an enormous amount of light into its environment, turning the night sky above into a seemingly blank canvas. Light Water Reactor Sustainability (LWRS) Program The Light Water Reactor Sustainability (LWRS) program conducts research to develop technologies and other solutions to improve the economics and reliability, sustain the safety, and extend the operation of our nation’s fleet of nuclear power plants. It has two objectives with respect to long-term operations: (1) to provide science- and technology-based solutions to industry to overcome the current labor-intensive business model and associated practices; and (2) to manage the aging of systems, structures, and components (SSCs) so nuclear power plants can continue to operate safely and cost-effectively. The Light Water Reactor Sustainability (LWRS) program is focused on the following three goals: Developing the fundamental scientific basis to understand, predict, and measure changes in materials and SSCs as they age in environments associated with continued long-term operations of existing nuclear power plants. Here’s everything you need to know about lightning, from how it forms to common myths and how to stay safe. Lightning flashes during a tropical storm in Guatemala. Photograph By Babak Tafreshi, Nat Geo Image Collection By National Geographic Staff Last updated July 21, 2025 Lightning flashing across a darkened sky makes an unforgettable image. With their drama and power, it’s no wonder people have infused them with symbolic meaning. They’re associated with mythological deities, such as Zeus and Thor, and even an emoji , in popular culture. In daily life, these electric currents can be dangerous, sparking intense forest fires and causing deaths. It doesn’t help that there are many myths about lightning behavior. From its causes to safety tips, here’s everything you need to know about these bolts from the blue. What is lightning and what causes it? Lightning is an electrical discharge caused by imbalances between storm clouds and the ground, or within the clouds themselves. Most occur within the clouds. During a storm, colliding particles of rain, ice, or snow inside storm clouds increase the imbalance between storm clouds and the ground, and often negatively charge the lower reaches of storm clouds. ( Summer storms can strike suddenly. Here’s what causes them .) Objects on the ground, like steeples, trees, and Earth itself, become positively charged. Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of murdering her three children, will face a retrial next year, a judge has said, after a jury deadlocked last time in a case that gripped the nation. The judge set a trial date for 29 March 2027, though the district attorney did not explicitly say what charges Clancy would face. Prosecutors said they wanted a jury trial, and the defence said they took that to mean Clancy, 36, would again face first-degree murder charges. Five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan were strangled at the family home on 24 January 2023. The defence argues she had severe postpartum psychosis. Petruska Abstract Linear motion components are widely used in antenna metrology positioning systems, but long motion ranges can reduce positioning accuracy due to the difficulty of eliminating rail component non-linearity. Further, offset device-under-test (DUT) mounting can magnify rotation errors arising from slight variations of rail parallelism not captured by a strictly linear motion model. We present methods to reduce position and rotation inaccuracy through kinematic calibration using a Legendre polynomial model. The motion range of the rail system is conditioned for use over an appropriate evaluation range. She is thinking about getting around more easily. The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast. For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient. "Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says. But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport. It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo. Long-Duration Energy Storage Background From providing critical backup power during natural disasters to supporting more renewable energy coming online, energy storage technologies make the grid more flexible and resilient. Today’s energy storage technologies are not sufficiently scaled or affordable enough to meet energy demand that fluctuates throughout the day and night. Long-duration energy storage (LDES) is a cost-effective option to increase grid reliability and resilience so that reliable, affordable electricity is available whenever and wherever to everyone. DOE defines LDES as storage systems capable of delivering electricity for 10 or more hours in duration. Program Overview The Long-Duration Energy Storage portfolio helps to advance LDES systems toward widespread commercial deployment. The goal of this portfolio is to fund projects that will overcome the technical and institutional barriers that exist for deployment, with a focus on different technology types for a diverse set of regions. The Milky Way arcs above the walls of a gorge, framed by the three bright stars of the Summer Triangle. BABAK TAFRESHI, National Geographic Image Collection By Stefanie Waldek Published August 20, 2026 Stargazing can feel overwhelming when you don’t know where to begin. But in August, three exceptionally bright stars offer an easy starting point. Vega, Deneb, and Altair form the Summer Triangle, an enormous star pattern that rises high in the evening sky across much of the Northern Hemisphere. Once you find it, the triangle can serve as a guide to nearby constellations, deep-sky objects, and the Milky Way. It is also one of the most photogenic regions of the summer sky in August. Here’s how to find the Summer Triangle—and photograph what surrounds it. How to Find the Summer Triangle The Summer Triangle is not a constellation, but an asterism, or a recognizable pattern of stars. Begin with Vega, one of the brightest stars visible from Earth. In mid-August, observers in the Northern Hemisphere can generally find it high overhead. Deneb appears to one side of Vega, while Altair lies farther away, creating a large, elongated triangle. Here's why it happens and where to look. Venus, the Pleiades star cluster, and the bright star Capella rise in the dawn sky above a tufa formation in California’s Mono Lake. BABAK TAFRESHI, National Geographic Image Collection By Stefanie Waldek Published November 12, 2026 Look low in the northeastern sky on an autumn evening, and you might spot something unusual: a bright star flashing red, green, and blue. That’s Capella, one of the brightest stars in the night sky. But despite appearances, the star isn’t actually changing colors. The dazzling display is an optical effect caused by starlight passing through Earth’s atmosphere. And Capella isn’t the only star that puts on this kind of show. “Stars appear to twinkle or shimmer in the night sky, but this is not an inherent trait of stars,” says Emily Watson, astrophysicist and planetarium supervisor at the U.S. Space & Rocket Center. “As the light from a star passes through different densities and temperatures within our atmosphere, the light bends in a process called refraction.” The color flashes happen because Earth’s atmosphere bends different wavelengths of light by different degrees. Two fists thud like anvils onto the wooden tabletop, and the old bones of the Rødbrygga pub shudder in protest. pages.text: Looking for whales—and awe—in Baja California | National Geographic TRAVEL Looking for whales—and awe—in Baja California The Gulf of California was once known as “the aquarium of the world.” But on a recent whale watching trip—and in an era where climate change is making its mark—our writer wonders if it still delivers. The Sea of Cortez is famous for its marine mammals, including fin, minke, humpback whales, seals, and sea lions, as well as common and bottlenose dolphins. Story and video by Kinsey Gidick Published May 15, 2026 When considering a trip to Baja, it’s nearly impossible to dodge the words of two famous men: Jacques Cousteau and John Steinbeck. The pioneering French oceanographer famously called the Gulf of California “the aquarium of the world.” Not surprisingly, that line shows up everywhere—typed into brochures and slipped into itineraries, hovering like a promise. Originally born from Afro-Colombian communities, cumbia spread across the Spanish-speaking world , acquiring distinct musical accents along the way. In Peru, cumbia became particularly popular among oil workers deep in the Amazon. And when Jorge Rodriguez Grández started Los Mirlos in his small hometown of Moyobamba, his band played a regional style called cumbia amazónica, easily identifiable by its electric, reverb-heavy, surf-rock guitar. Throughout their performance, these cultural ambassadors share stories and declare their love for cumbia and their tropical homeland. We are so fortunate to host and share with you a group of true pioneers and innovators who, over 50 years later, still effortlessly pump out cumbia grooves. pages.text: Los Tigres' Tiny Desk, explained : Alt.Latino : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player Los Tigres' Tiny Desk, explained : Alt.Latino Last week we published a Tiny Desk Concert that ended up being unusual for a few reasons. First of all, it was the final production of our sixth annual El Tiny series. This was a very emotional moment for a lot of reasons. People really love Los Tigres del Norte, to the point that playing their albums feels like sitting with family. And if you’ve seen the introduction I gave the band just before they played at the desk you can see that I wasn’t embarrassed to get emotional when I talked about what the band means to me. That emotional intro led to some changes in our process and format that resulted in a huge response from the audience that went viral. The result was a messy moment behind the scenes here at NPR and more than a little confusion for a lot of you. This week’s episode looks back at last week. First we want to share with you, directly from us, an explanation of what happened. But mostly we want to put the spotlight back on the band and their music because for decades they have been bringing out the kind emotions that got this whole thing started. Give it a listen and enjoy the music. Again. - Felix This podcast episode was produced by Noah Caldwell and edited by Jacob Ganz and Otis Hart. Suraya Mohamed is the executive producer of NPR Music. pages.text: Luxor's Temples Will Fall Into Darkness for Six Minutes During the 2027 Eclipse | National Geographic TRAVEL BEST OF THE WORLD In 2027, See Luxor in a New Light In addition to the total eclipse that will cast the ancient city in shadow, new hotels and other experiences offer fresh incentive to visit the sphinxes and temples on the banks of the Nile. In the early morning hours outside Luxor, it is common to see dozens of hot-air balloons carrying visitors above ongoing excavation work near the Hungarian Archeological Mission in Thebes. András Zoltai By Zoey Goto Published October 20, 2026 The six-minute “eclipse of the century” in August 2027 will bring an influx of astrotourists to Luxor, but the city has far more to offer than any single celestial event. Straddling both banks of the Nile, Egypt's ancient capital is entering a new chapter, with a host of high-profile openings and experiences to complement its Pharaonic wonders. The lavishly restored Mandarin Oriental Winter Palace and the new Four Seasons Hotel Luxor are both set to welcome guests next year. Also making its debut is the 80-passenger Guardian of the Nile, Egypt's first luxury tourist sleeper train, which will stop in Luxor on its way from Cairo to Aswan. Tour the 3,000-year-old temples of Karnak, then soar above them in a hot-air balloon. MA vs. MS Degrees: A Guide Written by Coursera Staff • Updated on Jun 21, 2026 Discover how earning an MA or an MS degree can bolster your subject knowledge and critical thinking skills, accelerate your career growth, and even lead to higher salaries. The Master of Arts (MA) and the Master of Science (MS) are both graduate degrees you can earn once you've completed your bachelor's degree. MA and MS degrees typically take the same amount of time to complete: between 18 months and two years.
